summary.text: Numerical weather prediction uses mathematical models of the atmosphere and oceans to forecast the weather from current conditions.
First tried in the 1920s, it gave realistic results only once computer simulation arrived in the 1950s, and today it needs some of the world's most powerful supercomputers.
Small errors in its chaotic equations grow over time, and its forecast skill reaches only about six days.

facts.label: First hand forecast
facts.value: Six hours ahead, taking at least six weeks

facts.label: Error growth
facts.value: Small errors double about every five days

facts.label: Chaos limit
facts.value: About 14 days, even with a flawless model

items.prompt: In the 1920s Lewis Fry Richardson worked out a six-hour forecast for two points in Europe entirely by hand. How long did the calculation take him?

options.label: About six minutes
About six hours
About six days
At least six weeks

items.explain: Richardson's hand-made six-hour forecast took at least six weeks; only computers brought the work below the length of the forecast period itself.

items.prompt: Imagine perfect observations fed into a flawless model. Why could it still not forecast accurately months ahead?

options.label: Computers can't store that much data
Chaos lets tiny errors keep growing
The oceans are left out of the model
Observations are only taken once a day

items.explain: The equations are chaotic and small errors grow with time, which limits accurate forecasts to about 14 days even with accurate input and a flawless model.

items.prompt: A forecast centre runs many forecasts, from one model or several, and compares them. What does it gain?

options.label: A gauge of how confident to be
A way to skip collecting observations
An end to the chaos in the equations
A single answer that is always right

items.explain: Ensemble forecasts analyse multiple forecasts to quantify uncertainty, gauge confidence and get useful results further ahead.

items.prompt: A model's raw output can't resolve some details right at ground level. How did forecasters deal with this in the 1970s and 1980s?

options.label: They launched far more weather balloons
They stopped forecasting near the ground
They built a statistical link to ground conditions
They ran the models backward in time

items.explain: Model output statistics (MOS) is a statistical relationship between a model's output and the conditions that then occur at the ground.

items.prompt: Before a model run, readings from balloons, satellites and aircraft are fed into it. What is that step for?

options.label: To grade yesterday's forecast
To set the starting state for the run
To rewrite the model's equations
To decide which country runs it

items.explain: Entering observations to create the initial conditions is called initialization; the data become the starting point for the forecast.

items.prompt: An atmospheric model is asked to forecast four different things. Where would it do worst?

options.label: How a wildfire behaves
Where a tropical cyclone will track
How air quality changes over a region
Broad weather patterns over a continent

items.explain: Models perform poorly with processes in a relatively constricted area, such as wildfires, while regional models have improved cyclone track and air quality forecasts.

paragraphs.heading: Forecasting with equations
paragraphs.text: Numerical weather prediction, or NWP, forecasts the weather by feeding current conditions into mathematical models of the atmosphere and oceans. The idea is to take a snapshot of the air at one moment, then apply the laws of fluid dynamics and thermodynamics, written as equations, to work out how it will look later. Loading observations into the model to set its starting state is called initialization.

paragraphs.heading: Where the data comes from
paragraphs.text: Models run in many countries take in observations from radiosondes, weather satellites and other systems. Radiosondes are devices carried by weather balloons that climb through the troposphere well into the stratosphere, measuring the air and sending the results to a fixed receiver. The World Meteorological Organization standardizes instruments, methods and timing worldwide. Because the observations are unevenly spaced, data assimilation checks their quality and turns them into values at points the model can use, and these become the forecast's starting point.

paragraphs.heading: Coping with uncertainty
paragraphs.text: The equations must be supplemented with parameterizations for things like solar radiation, clouds and rain, soil, vegetation and terrain. Model output also misses some details near the ground, so in the 1970s and 1980s a statistical link between model output and the conditions that follow at the surface was built, called model output statistics (MOS). Since the 1990s, ensemble forecasts, which analyze many forecasts from one model or several, have helped gauge confidence and stretch useful forecasts further ahead.

paragraphs.heading: From hand sums to ENIAC
paragraphs.text: In the 1920s Lewis Fry Richardson, using methods developed by Vilhelm Bjerknes, worked out by hand a six-hour forecast for two points in central Europe, which took him at least six weeks. In 1950 the ENIAC produced the first forecasts made by computer, using a much simplified version of the equations. In 1954 Carl-Gustav Rossby's group in Sweden used the same model for the first operational forecast, meaning a routine one for practical use. The United States followed in 1955 with a joint unit of its Air Force, Navy and Weather Bureau.

paragraphs.heading: Climate models
paragraphs.text: Models built on the same physics can produce either short-term forecasts or long-term climate predictions, and the latter are widely used to understand and project climate change. In 1956 Norman Phillips built a model that realistically showed monthly and seasonal patterns in the troposphere, the first successful climate model. In the late 1960s, NOAA's Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory built the first general circulation climate model to combine ocean and atmosphere.
